review_items.title: Chemours Fayetteville Works → DESCRIBED_BY → chemours-cd.pdf
review_items.detail: NER pulled The Chemours Company Fayetteville Works from the consent decree PDF and matched it to facility NCD844706749 on name + EPA ID. Any edge that crosses from an extracted document entity onto a ledger facility always sees a human — this is the edge the hero question ("what does the Chemours decree say, and are we accepting their waste?") rides on, so a wrong match is a wrong answer, not a cosmetic error.
evidence: extracted_entity=The Chemours Company Fayetteville Works; confidence=0.9

review_items.title: Stericycle Environmental Solutions — enforcement doc on a TRANSPORTER, not a generator
review_items.detail: Stericycle Environmental Solutions appears in the custody chain as a transporter (TRANSPORTS_TO VLS), and NER also linked it to a federal complaint + settlement. The document names the corporate entity; the graph holds the transporter handler. Attaching the enforcement to the hauling node is defensible but not certain — the complaint may concern a different Stericycle facility. A reviewer decides whether the DESCRIBED_BY edge attaches here.

review_items.title: Inbound-tonnage rollup mixes manifest tons with summary tons
review_items.detail: The SHIPS_TO.total_tons edge property is summed from e_manifest line quantities, while RCRA_Compliance_Summary carries a facility-level accepted-tonnage figure. They are close but not identical (rejected and residue manifests are treated differently). A measure that subtracts or compares the two is cross-basis and is never inferred — a human declares the basis or the validator blocks every use of it.
evidence: e_manifest rollup vs RCRA_Compliance_Summary accepted tonnage

review_items.title: Waste codes kept as a manifest attribute — promote to dimension nodes?
review_items.detail: Distinct WASTE CODE values (D/F/U/P series) are modelled as a multi-valued attribute on each Manifest, not as WasteCode nodes — a code carried on a row is an attribute of the shipment, not an entity with its own registry. 'Which generators send the most Land-Disposal-Restricted (LDR) waste?' still resolves, as a filter over that attribute. Promoting waste codes (or an LDR grouping) to dimension nodes is a modelling choice a reviewer may make for convenience, but the builder does not assume it — this is the correction to the earlier 'every column becomes a node' build.
evidence: waste_codes_seen rolled up on SHIPS_TO edges

review_items.title: Legacy generator name on 3 pre-2023 manifests — low-confidence SHIPS_TO match
review_items.detail: Three early manifests carry a generator name string that the fuzzy matcher tied to an EPA ID at 0.58 — below the 0.60 relationship floor. The name is a punctuation/spacing variant of an existing generator, but under the floor it does not auto-attach. Left unresolved, those three manifests' tonnage is orphaned from the generator's SHIPS_TO rollup.

pivot.title: Entity resolution: Texas Molecular LP vs VLS Texas Molecular
pivot.detail: Manifests shipped before 2023-01-05 carry Texas Molecular LP in DES FACILITY NAME; post-acquisition rows carry VLS Texas Molecular. Both resolve to EPA ID TXD000719518 via the alias table. Confidence is high, but an identity merge is never auto-applied — approving collapses the pre- and post-acquisition history onto one node and every rollup that cites either name inherits the merge.
pivot.why_pivot: Every inbound-flow row in this queue is measured against this facility’s history, so the queue cannot be read until the merge is settled.
evidence: entity_resolution: Texas Molecular LP -> FAC:TXD000719518 (alias table + EPA ID)

sanity_checks.question: What does the Chemours consent decree say, and are we accepting waste from that facility?
sanity_checks.verdict_body: The document node for chemours-cd.pdf is linked by DESCRIBED_BY to the Chemours Fayetteville Works facility, which is linked by SHIPS_TO to VLS Texas Molecular with tonnage and manifest count on the edge. Structured and unstructured data meet on one node — the traversal below is the whole point of the graph.
sanity_checks.plan: MATCH (d:Document {id:'DOC:chemours_cd'})<-[:DESCRIBED_BY]-(f:Facility)-[s:SHIPS_TO]->(vls:Facility {id:'FAC:TXD000719518'}) RETURN f, d, s.total_tons, s.manifests

sanity_checks.question: Trace manifest 346581037ELC cradle-to-grave: who generated it, who hauled it, when did we receive it?
sanity_checks.verdict_body: The manifest node carries GENERATED (from Arkema Crosby), TRANSPORTED (Sprint Waste Services, 5 days in possession) and RECEIVED_BY (VLS) edges. The chain is walkable node-by-node in custody order.
sanity_checks.plan: MATCH (gen:Facility)-[:GENERATED]->(m:Manifest {id:'MAN:346581037ELC'})-[:RECEIVED_BY]->(vls:Facility) MATCH (t:Facility)-[tr:TRANSPORTED]->(m) RETURN gen, t, tr.days, m, vls

sanity_checks.question: Which generators shipping to Deer Park are under active RCRA enforcement, and how much waste did we accept from them?
sanity_checks.verdict_body: Generator facilities carry ENFORCEMENT_AGAINST edges from Enforcement events and SHIPS_TO edges (manifests + tons) into VLS. The traversal joins the two so enforcement and accepted tonnage read on one path. Sub-graph shows three of the highest-exposure generators; the full query returns all 15.
sanity_checks.plan: MATCH (e:Enforcement)-[:ENFORCEMENT_AGAINST]->(f:Facility) MATCH (f)-[s:SHIPS_TO]->(vls:Facility {id:'FAC:TXD000719518'}) RETURN f, s.total_tons, s.manifests ORDER BY f.penalty_usd DESC

sanity_checks.question: Is 'Texas Molecular' the same facility as 'VLS Texas Molecular' — how does the system know?
sanity_checks.verdict_body: Three raw name strings resolve onto one facility node by alias table + EPA-ID match. The RESOLVES_TO sub-graph is the proof: the legacy pre-acquisition names and the current name all point at FAC:TXD000719518 with the method and confidence on each edge.

sanity_checks.question: Which generators send us the most Land-Disposal-Restricted (LDR) waste?
sanity_checks.verdict: Graph can answer this — LDR is a filter over a manifest attribute.
sanity_checks.verdict_body: Waste codes are a multi-valued attribute on each Manifest (and rolled up on the generator's SHIPS_TO edge), not WasteCode nodes. 'LDR' is a regulatory grouping of specific codes (D001, D008, D009, F-series...) applied as a filter over that attribute at query time — the same codes, no node to build. The traversal walks generator -> SHIPS_TO -> VLS and reads waste_codes_seen; per-manifest tonnage refines it. This is the corrected model: a code carried on a row is an attribute of the shipment, not an entity.

graph_use_cases.name: Hazardous waste compliance
graph_use_cases.business_need:
Cradle-to-Grave Compliance & Liability Intelligence — VLS Texas Molecular (Deer Park)
Framing. VLS-as-operator. VLS runs a RCRA-permitted Class I injection TSDF in Deer Park. Every load it accepts carries the generator’s liability with it. This use case unifies the inbound manifest stream, each generator’s and transporter’s federal compliance record, and public enforcement documents into one queryable model so VLS can see the risk it is taking on — before it accepts the next load.
Scope. Deer Park facility only. VLS Texas Molecular is always the receiving facility.
Problem. Manifest data, generator compliance history, and enforcement documents live in three disconnected places (BigQuery e-Manifest views, RCRAInfo, and PDF consent decrees). No one can answer ‘which of the generators shipping to us is under active enforcement, and how much waste did we take from them last quarter?’ without a manual, multi-day cross-reference.

blocks.title: Inbound tonnage by generator compliance status

blocks.markdown: The figure is high because the corridor's largest generators — the ones you take the most waste from — are also the ones with the longest compliance histories. Volume and risk are correlated here, which is the uncomfortable finding the CSO needs to carry into the boardroom.

ask_answers.question: Show me every rejected load and residue manifest, and which generators they came from.
ask_answers.summary: 26 rejected loads and 46 residue manifests over the full window, spread across high-volume generators.

blocks.markdown: Inbound acceptance-control view. Rejections and residue manifests are the data-quality signals an operations director watches — they flag loads that failed acceptance criteria or returned residue for re-manifesting.

Rejections (2.2% of loads) are spread across the high-volume generators rather than concentrated in one — no single generator is a systematic acceptance problem. Residue manifests (46) are routine re-manifesting of treatment residue, not a red flag in themselves.

ask_answers.question: Is 'Texas Molecular' the same facility as ‘Texas Molecular LP’ — how does the system know?
ask_answers.summary: Yes — same EPA ID (TXD000719518). The graph resolves the legacy and post-acquisition names to one facility node.

blocks.markdown: **Yes.** `Texas Molecular LP` (pre-2023) and `Texas Molecular` (post-acquisition, 2023-01-05) are the same physical site under one EPA ID, **`TXD000719518`**. Manifests shipped before the acquisition carry the legacy name in `DES FACILITY NAME`; the graph resolves every variant to a single facility node.

blocks.title: Name variants resolving to one node

blocks.markdown: **How it knows.** Resolution is anchored on the EPA ID (an exact match across all variants), reinforced by the alias table and a `RESOLVES_TO` edge from each legacy label to the canonical node. This is the trust moment for the CIO: the system doesn't guess from string similarity alone — it grounds the merge on a regulatory identifier.

ask_answers.question: What submission types make up our inbound manifests?
ask_answers.summary: About 69% FullElectronic, 21% Hybrid, the rest Data+Image or Image.

blocks.markdown: The inbound stream is predominantly fully electronic, which is what makes cradle-to-grave tracing reliable — paper and image submissions are the ones that degrade traceability.

ask_answers.question: What is the status breakdown of our inbound manifests?
ask_answers.summary: The large majority are Received; a small tail is Signed, Corrected or awaiting signature.

blocks.markdown: A high Received share is the healthy state — it means loads completed the chain of custody. The Corrected count is where post-receipt manifest edits happened, worth spot-checking for data-quality.

ask_answers.question: How long is waste typically in transit before we receive it?
ask_answers.summary: Most loads reach Deer Park within a week; the mode is 5-7 days.

blocks.markdown: Longer transit times cluster in the multi-transporter chains — each custody handoff adds roughly a day. The 8+ bucket is worth watching for any hauler consistently at the slow end.

ask_answers.question: What is our average transporter days-in-possession, and which chains are slowest?
ask_answers.summary: About 5 days on average; three-transporter chains run 1-2 days longer.

blocks.markdown: Days in possession rises with the number of custody handoffs. Single-transporter loads are fastest; the slowest chains are the three-transporter routes, typically the out-of-state shipments.

ask_answers.question: Which generators shipping to us are Large Quantity Generators (LQG)?
ask_answers.summary: Most corridor petrochemical generators are LQGs.

blocks.markdown: The bulk of your inbound tonnage comes from Large Quantity Generators (`FED_WASTE_GENERATOR=1`) — ExxonMobil Baytown, Pemex Deer Park, LyondellBasell Channelview, Arkema Crosby and the other major refineries and chemical plants. LQG status raises the regulatory bar on both the generator and the receiving TSDF.

ask_answers.question: Which generators sent us the most waste by tonnage?
ask_answers.summary: LyondellBasell Channelview Complex leads at 1,502.7 tons.

ask_answers.question: What is the total RCRA penalty exposure across all generators shipping to us?
ask_answers.summary: Roughly $2.05M in cumulative historical penalties, concentrated in the top three generators.

blocks.markdown: The figure is cumulative historical penalty across all inbound generators. It is concentrated: Arkema Crosby, ExxonMobil Baytown and J.R. Simplot alone make up over half.

ask_answers.question: What is our largest single inbound shipment?
ask_answers.summary: The largest single manifest is roughly 42 tons.

blocks.markdown: The single largest inbound manifest by quantity is around 42 tons of hazardous waste. Single-manifest quantities cluster well below that — the mean load is far smaller — so the largest shipments are outliers worth noting for handling capacity, not the norm.

ask_answers.question: How quickly do generators return to compliance after a violation?
ask_answers.summary: Return-to-compliance intervals range from ~30 to ~240 days.

blocks.markdown: Measured from `VIOL_DETERMINED_DATE` to `ACTUAL_RTC_DATE`, closure intervals span roughly 30 to 240 days. Lower-risk generators close fastest; the open (unreturned) violations are the ones with no `ACTUAL_RTC_DATE` at all — those are the live exposure, covered in the open-violation query.

ask_answers.question: What enforcement types appear most often in the compliance data?
ask_answers.summary: Informal actions and Notices of Violation dominate; formal penalty orders and CAFOs are rarer but larger.

blocks.markdown: The pattern is typical: most enforcement is informal (letters, notices), while the small number of formal actions — Administrative Penalty Orders, CAFOs, Consent Decrees — carry the large dollar penalties. The consent decrees and CAFOs are the ones that bridge to the uploaded document set.

ask_answers.question: Which comparator TSDFs could receive this waste besides us?
ask_answers.summary: Clean Harbors Deer Park, US Ecology Texas, Veolia Port Arthur and WM Disposal Services of Texas.

blocks.markdown: Comparators are included so the facility scorecard reads against peers — the clean $0-penalty record is only legible next to what other TSDFs carry.

ask_answers.question: How many residue manifests did we process?
ask_answers.summary: 46 residue manifests.

blocks.markdown: Residue manifests (`MANIFEST RESIDUE='Y'`) are routine re-manifesting of treatment residue for onward management — expected for an operating TSDF, not a red flag on their own.

ask_answers.question: What waste codes does Arkema Crosby typically ship?
ask_answers.summary: A mix of ignitable (D001), corrosive (D002) and spent-solvent (F001-F005) codes.

blocks.markdown: Arkema Crosby's manifests carry a characteristic-plus-solvent profile: **D001** (ignitable), **D002** (corrosive) and the **F001-F005** spent-solvent family. That mix is LDR-relevant, so their loads are among those where treatment-standard documentation matters most.

ask_answers.question: How current is the compliance data — when was the last evaluation recorded?
ask_answers.summary: The most recent evaluation across the corridor is in mid-2026.

blocks.markdown: Per-facility recency lives in `RCRA_Compliance_Summary.LAST_EVALUATION_DATE`. In production this refreshes on the RCRAInfo sync cadence; in the demo it is frozen consistent with the manifest window.

ask_answers.question: Can you show the full custody chain for a multi-transporter shipment?
ask_answers.summary: Yes — multi-hauler manifests list transporters in custody order.

blocks.markdown: Manifests with `TRANSPORTER_COUNT > 1` carry the haulers in custody order in `TRANSPORTER_NAMES` / `TRANSPORTER_IDS` (pipe-delimited). The graph turns each into a `TRANSPORTED` edge, so the chain is walkable node by node, not just readable as a string.

ask_answers.question: Which generators have violations noted but no enforcement action yet?
ask_answers.summary: Several mid-risk generators show a violation with no formal enforcement recorded.

blocks.markdown: These are generators where `FOUND_VIOLATION='Yes'` but `ENF_TYPE_DESC` is null — a violation was noted but not escalated to formal enforcement. They sit a tier below the penalty leaderboard but still warrant screening, because an un-escalated violation can still be open.

ask_answers.question: Which generator has the most violations overall?
ask_answers.summary: LyondellBasell Channelview and ITC Deer Park carry the most recorded violations.

blocks.markdown: Violation count and penalty rank are related but not identical — a generator can accumulate many minor violations without a large cumulative penalty, or a few serious ones with a large penalty. ITC Deer Park is high on both counts.

ask_answers.question: How do I know these answers are trustworthy?
ask_answers.summary: Every answer cites its source view and rows, and carries a confidence score.

blocks.markdown: Each response names the **source view and the rows** it was computed from, and carries a **confidence chip**. High-confidence answers (≥0.85) come from direct table lookups; medium and low scores flag estimation or joins across partial data. Nothing is asserted without a traceable path back to a source column — which is what separates this from a chatbot guessing over your data.

ask_answers.summary: 15 of 36 active generators carry enforcement history; screen open-violation shippers before acceptance.

suggestions.rationale: The tracking number is unique on both sides, so the enriched view is one row per manifest rather than a fan-out of them. Worth declaring because the generator, receiver and transporter profiles a question needs live on the enriched side while the shipment itself is on this one.

Both views are one row per facility on the same registry id, so this is a profile and its summary rather than a history. Declare it and a facility question can reach the rolled-up compliance standing without walking the line items.

The registry id is unique on the facility view and repeats across the line items, which is one facility to many evaluations, violations and enforcement actions. This is the join every "what is this facility's compliance record" question walks.

Many manifests to one facility. Note the shape of this extract before accepting it: the receiving id has exactly one distinct value across all 1,200 manifests, so every shipment here goes to the same TSDF — the cardinality is right, and it is right for a narrower reason than a fuller extract would give.

Both views carry the generator id and neither is unique on it — 36 generators across 1,200 rows on each side — so the join is genuinely many-to-many and would multiply rows if anything traversed it. Offered because the columns match, not because this is the join you want: the generator belongs on the facility view, and re-pointing it there is the likelier answer.
